description:
Alara is a high school senior interested in computer vision, robotics and space technology. 

Ranjitha is a lawyer and human-centered design engineer whose published research explores HCI and AI safety in high-stakes professions. She translates research, legal insight, and responsible design into practical tools for safer, more human-centered technology.

Maju works to increase equitable practices in organizations and increase collaboration amongst stakeholders in the global social impact space.
summary: HERMONA is an offline-first health monitoring prototype designed for female astronauts on long-duration missions. It combines wearable indicators, voluntary logged menstrual cycle and medication context, and each astronaut's personal baseline to identify sustained changes across several signals. Instead of giving medical data without explanations, HERMONA shows what changed, which inputs contributed, what data is missing, and which transparent rule produced its simulated recommendation. It then gives a clear next step: continue with monitoring, recover and recheck, or defer a demanding task and prepare a medical handoff. t runs locally and stays usable when communication with Earth is delayed or unavailable. NASA OSDR datasets and Human Research Program resources inform the monitored domains, mission context, and countermeasure follow-up. The demo runs on real two-week Apple Watch data and a self-logged menstrual cycle from a team member, read against her a terrestrial baseline with NASA datasets helping in evaluation and live monitoring. The surrounding Mars-transit scenario is clearly labeled synthetic.
details:
WHAT DOES IT DO?
HERMONA helps a female crew member in menstrual health monitoring and evaluation, along with behavioral health monitoring. It recommends whether she can continue with a demanding mission task, should recover and recheck, or should defer the task and prepare a medical handoff. The prototype evaluates factors like resting heart rate, HRV, sleep, activity, workload, wellbeing, bleeding history, and voluntary cycle or medication context against the astronaut's own baseline. It checks data quality and looks for sustained compound patterns rather than treating one unusual reading as proof of illness.

Every finding made based on daily check ins exposes its contributing measurements, missing or excluded inputs, evidence references, limitations, and the deterministic rule that produced the result. The same inputs therefore produce the same inspectable recommendation. A local-only AI chatbot explains these findings in plain terms acting like a health companion and reminder for health check-ins.

BENEFITS AND INTENDED IMPACT

  • It incorporates menstrual justice and provides a platform for women menstrual health monitoring and evaluation in space.
  • After more than 60 years of spaceflight, there has been inadequately testing of female reproductive health in space. The intended impact is to make women’s physiological health visible and actionable on long-duration missions and to help close the sex-data gap in spaceflight medicine.
  • It keeps relevant health context onboard when Earth cannot respond in real time, supporting a more inclusive evidence base and a safer path for the best-qualified crew members to participate in exploration missions.


HOW DOES IT WORK?

Hermona is a progressive web app that can work offline and incorporated privacy-by-design principles. Personal data is stored locally with IndexedDB, Apple Health exports can be parsed in the browser, and camera frames used for the gesture check-in are processed locally. For behavioral health, HERMONA also offers short recovery activities and nudges like paced-breathing resets, a guided body scan, and a lightweight focus mini-game that encourages rest and attention between check-ins. Users can inspect a de-identified research packet before choosing to queue or download it for later approved sharing. The Mars-transit demonstration uses clearly labeled synthetic data with counterfactual controls that let judges see how selected inputs change the simulated result.

HOW IS IT CREATIVE?

  • HERMONA pairs voluntarily logged cycle and medication context with wearable trends and NASA evidence, a combination no existing crew tool offers.
  • It supports hands-free, glove-friendly hand-gesture based check-ins and voice-based chat built for microgravity.
  • Optional on-device AI explains health data, including risks and emergencies in plain language.
  • Short gamified behavioral nudges exist to help astronauts rejuvenate.
  • NASA mission replay and counterfactual controls let users see how evidence and individual inputs affect the result instead of receiving a black-box score.

WHY IS THIS IMPORTANT?

We tried solving two challenges which make this issue important:

Challenge 1: “Women already manage periods in space with Oral Contraceptive Pills, so what’s the problem?”

Menstrual suppression is commonly used in spaceflight, and oral contraceptive pills have historically been the most commonly reported method. NASA research notes that OCP use doubles terrestrial VTE or blood-clot risk. That same research also states that current risk models do not include the spaceflight environment or associated physiological changes, including cephalic fluid shifts and lower-limb inactivity. The management plan may be selected before launch, but physiology, workload, sleep, medication use, and mission conditions continue to change. On a Mars-class mission, communication delay means reassessment cannot depend on an immediate answer from Earth. The problem is not managing periods. It is maintaining an in-flight feedback loop around the management choice and the cardiovascular context that may accompany it. (NASA NTRS 20140016949 and 20150008176)

Challenge 2: “Are terrestrial vs space, and female vs male, datasets different?”

HERMONA addresses the following gaps here: First is the sex-data gap: spaceflight studies have historically relied on male-dominated samples, and NASA's 2024 Women's Health in Spaceflight review says research defining female biological responses remains limited and is not yet robust enough for sex-specific prediction. Second is the environment gap: terrestrial VTE models do not account for the spaceflight environment. Female-specific, space-aware risk therefore remains a real blind spot. HERMONA brings the best available NASA and terrestrial evidence into an explainable, personal-baseline workflow, identifies whether evidence comes from human spaceflight, analog, or animal studies, and creates structured longitudinal logs that could support approved future research. (NASA NTRS 20240006986)

WHAT FACTORS DID WE CONSIDER?

We considered communication delays, intermittent connectivity, limited crew time, privacy, individual variation, missing or low-quality readings, menstrual suppression and medication context, sleep and workload, cardiovascular and behavioral changes, accessibility in microgravity, and alert fatigue. We also designed for explainability and human medical oversight. Each risk flag must show where it came from and human analogs remain clearly identified. Research provenance, local data control, responsible AI disclosure, false-alert and missed-alert testing, and a path to aerospace-clinician and analog-mission review shaped the prototype.

CODING LANGUAGE AND TOOLS USED:

HERMONA was built with React 18, TypeScript, Vite, Tailwind CSS, React Router, Dexie and IndexedDB, Recharts, MediaPipe Tasks Vision, the Chrome Prompt API, and Vitest. Our next goal is aerospace-clinician review of this prototype followed by approved sensor integration, false-alert and missed-alert testing, human-factors evaluation, and an analog-mission study.
dataRefs: NASA OSDR SpaceX Inspiration4 mission collection — mission timeline and de-identified longitudinal human spaceflight data used to structure Hermona’s mission replay.

NASA OSDR GLDS-51 - Woman skeletal muscle transcriptome with bed rest and countermeasures. HERMONA uses this female-specific analog evidence to prioritize activity, recovery, and countermeasure follow-up. It does not provide wearable time series or clinical thresholds.

NASA OSDR GLDS-195 - Effects of 21 days of bed rest on human skeletal muscle gene expression. The app displays this male dataset beside GLDS-51 to make the sex-data gap visible and to provide deconditioning context.
